sentences.text: Baptornis was a genus of aquatic birds that lived in the Late Cretaceous, specifically from the Coniacian to the Campanian stages, between 89.8 and 72.2 million years ago.
This bird possessed a markedly elongated neck compared to its relatives, a feature that allowed it to strike fish with its sharp beak.
Weighing about 7 kg and measuring 1 meter in length, Baptornis had small sharp teeth covering its jaws, unlike modern birds.
Its lower legs were flush against its body with feet stretched sideways, making it unable to stand upright and likely finding walking on land difficult.
Baptornis held prey in its beak like mergansers rather than spearing it like darters, a method useful for holding fish firmly which made up most of its diet.
Coprolites associated with Baptornis contain remains of the sabre-toothed fish Enchodus, providing the only certain record of food for the Hesperornithes group.
Although its tiny wings only served to propel them forward while swimming, the bird was an excellent swimmer that used its huge webbed feet for propulsion.
Othniel Charles Marsh discovered the first fossils of Baptornis in the 1870s, making it one of the first Mesozoic birds known to science, alongside Archaeopteryx.
The type species of the genus is Baptornis advenus, and there are 10 recorded fossil occurrences of the animal in the Paleobiology Database.

Baptornis was excellently adapted for swimming and diving but thought to be clumsy on land, yet it was a skilled underwater predator capable of maneuvering well by twisting and turning quickly while chasing prey.
The bird had a torpedo-like profile and was aerodynamic, facilitating its movements in water, while its flat sternum indicates that the muscles controlling its wings were small and weak.
Huge webbed feet provided almost all the propulsive force when diving or swimming, suggesting the bird likely spent most of its life swimming in water or floating on the sea.

Baptornis was likely constantly threatened by large marine reptiles like mosasaurs living beneath the sea surface, so it probably spent most of its life in open sea and only went to land to lay eggs and raise its young.
The family Baptornithidae was established for Baptornis due to its peculiar characteristics among Hesperornithes, and the genus belongs to the parent group Baptornithidae.

Parascaniornis stensioi, previously thought to be a flamingo or loon, is now considered to belong with Baptornis, while the classification of Neogaeornis is debated; it might be a baptornithid or related to modern Gaviiformes or Procellariiformes.
The Paleobiology Database classifies Baptornis under the class Reptilia.

Fossils of the type species Baptornis advenus were found in Kansas, an area covered by the shallow Western Interior Seaway, and fossils are found in limestone rocks that typically form at shorelines, indicating a coastal habitat.
Baptornis is also known from Sweden and possibly occurred throughout the Holarctic region.
